newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan scandal to overshadow brokerage share prices.
newsitem.headline: Japan scandal to overshadow brokerage share prices.

text.p: Japan's widening payoffs scandal deepens concerns over competitiveness in the country's top brokerage houses and is likely to put a cloud over their share price outlook, analysts said on Wednesday.

News of Tokyo prosecutors' raid on Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd pierced the stock market on Wednesday ahead of the long-awaited announcement of administrative punishment on giant brokerage Nomura Securities Co Ltd.

After the market closed, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) ordered the suspension of key parts of Nomura and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank's (DKB) businesses for various durations, some as long as a year. It included a halt to Nomura's own-account stock-related dealing from August 6 to December 31.
Both firms were also barred from underwriting government bonds until the end of this year.

"It should take quite long time for them to regain the trust of their customers," said Yushiro Ikuyo, first vice president at Smith Barney International Inc. "It is likely to undermine their profitability slowly."
The news on Wednesday pushed down shares amid worries that more big brokerages could be involved in the payoff scandal.
The Nikkei 225 index lost 189.92 points or 0.93 percent to close at 20,212.82.

Shares of Yamaichi tumbled in the heaviest trade in the first section of the Tokyo bourse, briefly sliding as low as 275 yen, the lowest price this year. It ended down 21 yen, or 6.98 percent, at 280 yen.
Other "Big Four" brokerages were also depressed by the news. Daiwa Securities Co Ltd was down 40 yen at 825 yen, and Nikko Securities Co Ltd fell 21 yen to 670 yen.
Although the immediate impact will be limited, the widening scandal of major brokers may suck energy out of the stock market over a longer period, brokers said.

"If dealing for their own accounts, for example, were to be suspended for all four brokerages, turnover would diminish even more and hurt investor sentiment in general," said Shinichi Ichikawa, a strategist at Credit Lyonnais Securities.

Kiyoshi Kimura, general manager of research at Societe Generale Securities, said now that the official penalties on Nomura have been announced, it would prompt institutional investors to halt their business with Japan's largest brokerage.
"The situation surrounding the scandal is quite unclear and it is too early to say that the market has factored in the negative impact," Kimura added.
But at least one analyst now rated Nomura a buy. Robert Garone, analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson Securities, said the shares were now attractive after the announcement of the penalties.
"In the long run, the company will remain the strongest brokerage in the Tokyo market after the ongoing deregulation," he said.
